slides.title: Philosophy in India and China
slides.question: How should we live, and who are we really?
slides.sub: The Upanishads and the Buddha; Confucius, Laozi and the Hundred Schools
slides.notes:
Philosophy did not begin only in Greece. At almost the same time, thinkers in India and China asked equally deep questions, often with very different emphases. Indian philosophy asked what the self really is and how to escape suffering. Chinese philosophy asked how people can live together in harmony, in families and states.
Tonight we visit both traditions, see where they agree and differ, and ask what they still offer us.
Next: a surprising coincidence in world history.

slides.title: The Axial Age: many beginnings at once
slides.sub: Karl Jaspers’ name for c. 800–200 BCE
slides.caption: Separate, but similar
slides.text: In a few centuries, with little or no contact, Greece, Israel, Persia, India and China produced the traditions that still shape most of humanity. Each moved from myth and ritual towards argument, ethics and inner reflection.
slides.notes:
The German philosopher Karl Jaspers called the period from about 800 to 200 BCE the Axial Age, because so much of human thought turns on it. Socrates, the Hebrew prophets, Zoroaster, the authors of the Upanishads, the Buddha, Mahavira, Confucius and Laozi all lived or were remembered in roughly this window.
Historians debate how real the pattern is, and there was little contact between these regions. But the parallel is striking: in each place, thinkers turned from ritual and myth towards argument, ethics and the inner life.
Next: three different starting questions.

slides.title: Three traditions, three starting questions
slides.sub: A simplification, but a useful one

cols.label: Greece
cols.title: What is the world made of?
cols.text: From nature to knowledge to the good life, by argument.

cols.label: India
cols.title: What is the self, and how do we escape suffering?
cols.text: Philosophy as a path to liberation.

cols.label: China
cols.title: How should we live together?
cols.text: Philosophy as the art of family, government and harmony.

slides.bottom: All three ask about the good life; they differ in where they look first.
slides.notes:
This is a simplification, but it helps. Greek philosophy often started from nature and argument. Indian philosophy usually treated philosophy as a path to liberation from suffering and rebirth. Chinese philosophy was intensely practical and social: how should a ruler govern, how should children treat parents, how can a society be in harmony?
All three cared about the good life. They simply began from different questions.
Next: India’s oldest philosophical texts.

slides.title: The Upanishads: four ideas that shaped India
slides.sub: c. 800–300 BCE: ‘sitting down near’ a teacher

cols.label: Brahman
cols.title: One ultimate reality
cols.text: Behind all things is one reality, as gold lies behind ring, bangle and coin.

cols.label: Ātman
cols.title: The true self
cols.text: Not the body or the mind, but the witness that can never be seen, as the eye can’t see itself.

cols.label: Karma
cols.title: You become what you do
cols.text: Actions shape character and future lives.

cols.label: Mokṣa
cols.title: Liberation
cols.text: Freedom from the cycle of rebirth, as a river reaches the sea.

slides.bottom: ‘Tat tvam asi’: you are that. The deepest self and ultimate reality are one.
slides.notes:
The Upanishads are dialogues and teachings attached to India’s oldest scriptures, the Vedas. Four ideas run through them. Brahman, the one reality behind everything. Ātman, the true self, the seer that can never be seen. Karma, the law that actions shape what we become. And mokṣa, liberation from the cycle of rebirth.
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad a father asks his son to dissolve salt in water: the salt is invisible yet everywhere. ‘You are that,’ he says: your true self is identical with ultimate reality. Later, Śaṅkara built his Advaita, or non-dual, philosophy on this.
Next: a prince who left home.

slides.title: The Buddha’s Four Noble Truths
slides.sub: The first sermon at Sarnath, c. 5th century BCE

steps.title: Suffering (dukkha)
steps.text: Life is unsatisfying: even good things change and end.

steps.title: Its cause
steps.text: Craving: grasping at pleasure, existence and self.

steps.title: Its end
steps.text: Nirvana: the fire of craving blown out.

steps.title: The path
steps.text: The Eightfold Path: right view, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration.

slides.bottom: Like a doctor: diagnosis, cause, prognosis, treatment.
slides.notes:
Siddhārtha Gautama, the Buddha, taught as a doctor treats a patient. First, the diagnosis: life is dukkha, unsatisfying, because everything we hold changes. Second, the cause: craving and grasping. Third, the prognosis: suffering can end; nirvana literally means ‘blowing out’, like a flame. Fourth, the treatment: the Eightfold Path of wisdom, ethics and meditation.
Next: three marks of existence.

slides.title: The three marks of existence

cols.label: Anicca
cols.title: Impermanence
cols.text: Everything changes: leaves, bodies, moods, empires.

cols.label: Dukkha
cols.title: Unsatisfactoriness
cols.text: Even the best holiday has its last evening.

cols.label: Anattā
cols.title: No fixed self
cols.text: A forest is just trees; a person is five changing ‘heaps’ with no owner behind them.

slides.bottom: Compare Hume, 2,200 years later: looking inward, he found only a bundle of perceptions.
slides.notes:
The Buddha taught that all conditioned things share three marks. They are impermanent. They are unsatisfying, because they don’t last. And they lack a fixed self: a person is made of five ‘heaps’ of body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness, with no hidden owner. This directly challenged the Upanishads’ ātman.
David Hume reached a strikingly similar view in the 1730s, when he looked inward for his self and found only a bundle of perceptions.
Next: the middle way.

slides.title: The Middle Way: not too tight, not too loose

challenge.title: Two dead ends
challenge.text: Chasing pleasure doesn’t free you. Years of starving himself as an ascetic didn’t free the Buddha either.

answer.title: The middle
answer.text: A lute string tuned too tight snaps; too loose, it won’t play. The mind needs the right tension.

open.title: Compare Aristotle
open.text: Virtue as a mean between extremes appears in both traditions, with different goals: liberation versus flourishing.

slides.bottom: Nāgārjuna later extended the middle way to metaphysics: things neither simply exist nor simply don’t.
slides.notes:
Before his awakening, the Buddha tried both extremes: a prince’s luxury and an ascetic’s starvation. Neither worked. The middle way is like tuning a stringed instrument: neither too tight nor too loose.
This invites comparison with Aristotle’s doctrine of the mean. Both see virtue between extremes, but the Buddha aims at liberation, Aristotle at flourishing in a city. Later, the philosopher Nāgārjuna applied the middle way to existence itself: things are empty of independent existence, yet not nothing.
Next: the variety of Indian schools.

slides.title: A rich family of schools, arguing for centuries
slides.sub: Indian philosophy was a debate, not a single view

items.caption: Nyāya
items.text: Logic and the sources of knowledge

items.caption: Madhyamaka (Nāgārjuna)
items.text: Everything is empty of fixed essence

items.caption: Yoga (Patañjali)
items.text: Stilling the movements of the mind

slides.bottom: Even the materialist Cārvāka school, which denied rebirth and God, was argued with seriously.
slides.notes:
Indian philosophy is often imagined as one mystical view. In fact it was a long, sharp debate among schools. Buddhists denied a lasting self; Advaita Vedānta said the self is Brahman; Jains taught radical non-violence and that truth has many sides; the Nyāya school developed logic and a theory of the sources of knowledge; Nāgārjuna argued that everything is empty of fixed essence; Patañjali’s Yoga taught disciplined stilling of the mind. The materialist Cārvākas rejected the whole idea of rebirth.
Next: China, and Confucius.

slides.title: Confucius: becoming fully human through relationships

cols.label: Ren
cols.title: Humaneness
cols.text: ‘Do not impose on others what you would not want yourself’ (15.24).

cols.label: Li
cols.title: Ritual and courtesy
cols.text: Bowing, mourning, greeting: forms that shape feeling.

cols.label: Xiao
cols.title: Filial piety
cols.text: Goodness starts at home, with care for parents.

cols.label: Junzi
cols.title: The exemplary person
cols.text: Learns all life and leads by example, not force.

slides.bottom: ‘Govern by virtue and the people will gather round you, like the stars round the pole star’ (2.1).
slides.notes:
Confucius taught in the small state of Lu during an age of disorder. His goal was to restore harmony by cultivating good people. Ren, humaneness, is the central virtue, summed up in his version of the golden rule. Li, ritual, includes all respectful forms of behaviour that shape our feelings. Xiao, filial piety, makes the family the school of virtue. And the junzi, the exemplary person, leads by example rather than punishment.
Next: a great debate about human nature.

slides.title: Is human nature good or bad?
slides.sub: The great debate of the Confucian school

a.name: Mencius
a.label: Nature is good
a.lead: Everyone would feel alarm seeing a child about to fall into a well. We have four sprouts of virtue.
points: Bad environments stunt it, like a bare mountain

b.name: Xunzi
b.label: Nature is bad
b.lead: We are born with selfish desires. Goodness is made, like straightening crooked wood.
points: Effort, not nature, makes us good

slides.bottom: Both agree anyone can become a sage; they disagree about whether the work is growing or carving.
slides.notes:
Mencius, a century after Confucius, argued that human nature is good. Anyone who sees a toddler about to fall into a well feels alarm, without thinking about reward. That shows we have ‘sprouts’ of compassion, shame, respect and right judgment, which grow if nourished. Bad people are like Ox Mountain, whose forests were cut and grazed bare.
Xunzi replied that our nature is bad: we are born wanting gain and pleasure. Goodness is an achievement, made through ritual and teachers, as crooked wood is straightened with steam. Both agree that anyone can become a sage.
Next: a very different path, the Dao.

slides.title: Daoism: follow the Way, don’t force it

cols.label: Dao
cols.title: The Way
cols.text: ‘The Dao that can be spoken is not the constant Dao.’ The nameless source of all things.

cols.label: Wu wei
cols.title: Effortless action
cols.text: Water is soft, yet wears away rock by flowing around it.

cols.label: Pu
cols.title: The uncarved block
cols.text: Return to simplicity before society carves us into shapes.

cols.label: Zhuangzi
cols.title: The butterfly dream
cols.text: Am I a man dreaming of a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming of a man?

slides.bottom: ‘The best rulers, the people barely know they exist’ (Daodejing 17).
slides.notes:
Daoists criticised Confucians for too much effort and too many rules. The Daodejing, traditionally by Laozi, speaks of the Dao, the Way, the nameless source of all things. Its key practice is wu wei, effortless action: like water, which is soft yet carves rock. Pu, the uncarved block, is the simplicity we had before society shaped us.
Zhuangzi added humour and scepticism: his butterfly dream asks how we know which state is real. Compare the Confucian who carves himself with the Daoist who returns to the uncarved block.
Next: the Hundred Schools.

slides.title: The Hundred Schools: four answers to disorder
head: School
Key idea
How to govern
rows: Cultivate virtue through ritual and relationships
Follow the natural Way; don’t force
By clear laws, rewards and harsh punishments
slides.bottom: The Legalists united China in 221 BCE; the Han dynasty then made Confucianism official, for two thousand years.
slides.notes:
In the Warring States period, seven states fought for survival and many thinkers offered cures. Confucians stressed virtue and ritual. Daoists urged simplicity. Mohists taught impartial care and judged every custom by its benefit. Legalists like Han Feizi said people only respond to reward and punishment.
The state of Qin used Legalism to unify China in 221 BCE, building the terracotta army along the way. But the Qin collapsed quickly, and the Han dynasty adopted Confucianism, which shaped Chinese government for two thousand years.
Next: how these ideas travelled.

slides.title: Ideas on the move
slides.sub: How the traditions met each other and the world

events.title: Buddhism reaches China
events.text: Along the Silk Road; it blends with Daoism into Chan (Zen).

events.title: Neo-Confucianism
events.text: Zhu Xi answers Buddhism with li and qi; his commentaries rule the exams.

events.title: Dōgen and Zen in Japan
events.text: Practice is not a ladder but enlightenment itself.

events.title: The Upanishads reach Europe
events.text: Schopenhauer reads them nightly: ‘the consolation of my life’.

slides.bottom: Philosophy has always been a conversation across cultures.
slides.notes:
These traditions did not stay put. Buddhism travelled from India to China in the first century CE, where it met Daoism and became Chan, known in Japan as Zen. Dōgen brought it to Japan in the 1200s. Neo-Confucians like Zhu Xi answered Buddhism with their own metaphysics of pattern and energy, li and qi. In the nineteenth century the Upanishads reached Europe in translation, and Schopenhauer read them every night.
Next: what we can learn.

slides.title: Different starting points, shared questions
questions: Is there a true self behind your thoughts and feelings?
Is goodness grown from nature, or carved by effort?
Should we strive harder, or learn when not to force?
slides.line: Philosophy is a world conversation, not a Greek monologue.
slides.notes: The traditions of India and China ask the same big questions as Greece, about the self, goodness and the good life, but from different angles. Studying them side by side shows which of our own assumptions are really universal.

slides.title: Discussion: bring the theory back to real life
questions: Which of the Four Noble Truths do you find most convincing, and which least?
Are people basically good, like Mencius says, or made good, like Xunzi says?
When is ‘not forcing it’ wise, and when is it just lazy?
slides.line: Give an example from your own life first.
